show_statement: This is a show about one body and a hundred bodies, and it keeps rebuilding the same sentence out of scaffolding: cream uniforms swarm a cage, something red gets on top of it, everyone else stays underneath. The cages are the whole argument — portable prisons on casters that the corps builds, climbs, rides, and finally abandons. What it's after is the moment a crowd becomes a structure, and it gets there most honestly when the structure is half-built and the swarm is still visibly a swarm (84 over 90, if I'm being strict with myself, which the ranking says I'm not). The color coding is blunt — cream is order, red-orange is the thing order is containing — but blunt is not the same as wrong, and when the entire guard falls at once at 582 while the horn line doesn't flinch, the bluntness pays off. The masked/unmasked bookend is the only quiet idea in it, and it's the best one. The cap bites here, badly. Losing 738 hurts most: the horn line frontal, arms out, the loudest picture in the set — cut because 270 says the same thing colder and emptier, and cold won. I'm also sorry to lose 162, the only frame that shows how much unused stadium this show is playing into, and 642, bass drums running past lounging guard members, which is the funniest accidental composition of the twenty-five. 114 and 336 both want to be the aerial-chaos frame and only one survived. 504 and 522 are the same beat photographed twice; the cap simply deleted the duplicate rather than making me choose, which is the cap doing my thinking for me and I resent it mildly.

keepers.reason: The show's whole thesis in one legible picture: a mass of bodies fused to a cage, one red figure standing on the lid. Empty stadium, championship banner, no crowd to soften it. If the show has a poster, this is it — and the fact that it looks designed rather than discovered is the trade it makes.

Every guard member horizontal in mid-fall while the horn line stays vertical and playing. This is the only frame where the two castes of the show touch and neither yields. It works because nobody is caught at the same angle — it reads as collapse, not choreography, for about half a second.

Same man, same box, mask off. Ends the show by revealing there was a face the whole time. It is the least spectacular image in the set and the only one that changes the meaning of another image retroactively.

The unfinished cage-climb. Bodies still scrambling, one red figure not yet planted, the form visibly under construction. Structurally weaker than 90 and more truthful than 90 — I keep both because the pair is the argument, but this is the one I'd stare at.

Overhead, the cages become a floor plan and the performers become traffic. Proves the props were designed as architecture first and set second. Also the only frame where the show looks like a diagram of itself, which is either its cleverest moment or its most airless.

The concept steps aside and a horn arc just plays into an empty house. No cages, no red, no idea — just deployment. Keeping it because a show this conceptual needs one frame that proves it can shut up, and because the vacant seats do more emotional work than any prop here.
Tight on one player, mesh sleeves, silver bell, a red body blurred out of frame behind him. The only frame with a pulse rate. Everything else in this set is composition; this is a person straining.

The masked opener. Reads as a ringmaster and functions as a lock — you spend the next twelve minutes waiting for the face. Slightly overdressed in a show that is otherwise about uniformity, which is exactly why it works as the exception.

Red floods the field and the cream ranks stop being ranks. The widest evidence that the containment fails. It's a messy frame and I'm keeping the mess — the show's tidy frames already have four representatives above this one.

Ground littered with instruments and bodies, one figure raised on the last cage with an arm up. A curtain call staged as an aftermath. Sentimental, and it earns it because everything horizontal in the frame was vertical ninety seconds ago.
